title: Giant Steps and Xandu crowned nation’s best Chardonnay and Cabernet
summary:
The Giant Steps 2024 Tarraford Vineyard Chardonnay from the Yarra Valley and the Xanadu 2024 Cabernet Sauvignon from Margaret River have been named Australia's best Chardonnay and Cabernet Sauvignon respectively at the 2026 James Halliday Australian Chardonnay & Cabernet Challenge. It was a landmark year for Xanadu, which took home three trophies: ‘Best Cabernet Sauvignon’, the ‘Margaret River Regional Trophy for Cabernet Sauvignon’, and the inaugural ‘Wine of Provenance Trophy for Cabernet Sauvignon’ with its Reserve Cabernet.

The post Giant Steps and Xandu crowned nation’s best Chardonnay and Cabernet appeared first on Winetitles.
content:
The Giant Steps 2024 Tarraford Vineyard Chardonnay from the Yarra Valley and the Xanadu 2024 Cabernet Sauvignon from Margaret River have been named Australia’s best Chardonnay and Cabernet Sauvignon respectively at the 2026 James Halliday Australian Chardonnay & Cabernet Challenge.

It was a landmark year for Xanadu, which took home three trophies: ‘Best Cabernet Sauvignon’, the ‘Margaret River Regional Trophy for Cabernet Sauvignon’, and the inaugural ‘Wine of Provenance Trophy for Cabernet Sauvignon’ with its Reserve Cabernet.

Shaw + Smith claimed the inaugural ‘Wine of Provenance Trophy for Chardonnay’ with its M3 Chardonnay.

This year’s challenge attracted close to 500 entries from 49 regions across Australia, with Chardonnay entered from 30 regions and Cabernet Sauvignon from 19. Judged over two days, the challenge gave the judging panel a first look at many wines from the 2025 vintage.

Regional trophies were awarded to Chardonnays from 10 regions and Cabernet Sauvignon from 6 regions, recognising the highest-scoring wine from each region at 95 points or above.

To mark 15 years of the challenge, 2026 saw the introduction of two new trophies: the ‘Chardonnay Wine of Provenance’ and the ‘Cabernet Sauvignon Wine of Provenance’. Each entry was a set of three wines from the same label, spanning at least eight vintages with at least three years between any two wines. Unlike the rest of the challenge, these classes were judged as one national group rather than by region, with judges looking for “longevity and consistency of quality and style as well as gold medal quality”.

Wine Yarra Valley launched the Chardonnay Challenge in 2012, and the Cabernet Challenge followed in 2016 in Margaret River. Since 2021, the James Halliday Australian Chardonnay & Cabernet Challenge has been “a joint endeavour between Wine Yarra Valley and Margaret River Wine, and an independent show proudly bearing the name of James Halliday AM”.

title: Central Otago wineries head to Australia for ‘Pure Pours’ festival
summary:
Following sold-out events across Australia in 2025, ‘Pure Pours: Central Otago Wine Festival’ is returning this October, bringing an expanded line-up of 22 Central Otago wineries touring Sydney, Melbourne and Brisbane. Each city will host a roaming tasting festival “where guests can sip, swirl and compare wines from across the region”. “Bringing our wines to Australia gives us the chance to connect directly with wine lovers and share what makes Central Otago such a unique place to grow grapes and make wine,” said Carolyn Murray, general manager of the Central Otago Winegrowers Association. “After the response to our 2025 events, we’re excited to return with even more wineries, offering more for the Australian public to discover.”

The post Central Otago wineries head to Australia for ‘Pure Pours’ festival appeared first on Winetitles.
content:
The event kicks off this weekend. Image credit @amar.gera

Following sold-out events across Australia in 2025, ‘Pure Pours: Central Otago Wine Festival’ is returning this October, bringing an expanded line-up of 22 Central Otago wineries touring Sydney, Melbourne and Brisbane.

Each city will host a roaming tasting festival “where guests can sip, swirl and compare wines from across the region”.

“Bringing our wines to Australia gives us the chance to connect directly with wine lovers and share what makes Central Otago such a unique place to grow grapes and make wine,” said Carolyn Murray, general manager of the Central Otago Winegrowers Association.

“After the response to our 2025 events, we’re excited to return with even more wineries, offering more for the Australian public to discover.”

Pure Pours brings the region’s winemakers and winery teams together under one roof, which organisers say presents “a rare chance for Australian wine lovers to meet the people behind the labels and taste their wines side by side”.

“With 90+ wines on pour, it’s about as close as you can get to experiencing Central Otago without boarding a plane,” they said.

The festival will kick-off this weekend on Saturday 17 October in Sydney at The International from 1pm to 4pm. Then, Melbourne will host on Monday 19 October from 5pm to 8pm at Victoria by Farmer’s Daughters. Finally, the Brisbane event will be held at The Lodge on James Street on Tuesday 20 October from 5pm to 8pm.

Tickets are $60 per person plus a booking fee, with more information available here.

title: 2026 New Zealand Winegrowers’ Mentoring Programme kicks off
summary:
The New Zealand Winegrowers’ Mentoring Programme has gotten underway.
New Zealand Winegrowers (NZW) said the program “demonstrates there are many experienced industry leaders willing to give their time to provide others with encouragement, inspiration and support”. Mentors are matched with mentees who are looking to take the next step in their careers and to progress in the industry. The programme is open to anyone working in New Zealand’s wine industry, working in all roles including viticulture, winemaking, operations, laboratory, sales, marketing, cellar door and general management. Over the years, the programme has seen some real success stories, with participants gaining much from the experience, explained Nicky Grandorge, leadership & communities manager at New Zealand Winegrowers. “It’s fantastic to see people across the industry generously sharing their time, knowledge and experience,” said Grandorge.

content:
Amy Lister, Sophie Matthews, Gemma Blair, Charlotte Read, Jody Pagey, Fiona Fenwick, Sara Macdonald, Rosie Jaffe-Menzies and Nicky Grandorge. Image supplied

The New Zealand Winegrowers’ Mentoring Programme has gotten underway.

New Zealand Winegrowers (NZW) said the program “demonstrates there are many experienced industry leaders willing to give their time to provide others with encouragement, inspiration and support”.

Mentors are matched with mentees who are looking to take the next step in their careers and to progress in the industry. The programme is open to anyone working in New Zealand’s wine industry, working in all roles including viticulture, winemaking, operations, laboratory, sales, marketing, cellar door and general management.

Over the years, the programme has seen some real success stories, with participants gaining much from the experience, explained Nicky Grandorge, leadership & communities manager at New Zealand Winegrowers.

“It’s fantastic to see people across the industry generously sharing their time, knowledge and experience,” said Grandorge.

“That spirit of collaboration is very special. It strengthens our industry and helps talented people continue to grow.

“As well as highlighting the New Zealand wine industry’s supportive community, the programme reflects the ambition and passion of people wanting to progress. It’s a very positive programme.”

The 2026 mentors generously volunteering their time are: Amy Lister, Yealands; Sophie Matthews, Wineworks; Gemma Blair, Hillebrand Gori; Charlotte Read, New Zealand Winegrowers; Jody Pagey, VinPro, Sara Macdonald, Radburnd Cellars; Rosie Jaffe-Menzies, Carrick; Anna Remond, OTU Wines; Kate Lattey, No.287 Vineyard; and Jane Hunter, Hunter’s Wines.

This year’s induction workshop for mentors, was led by author and coach Fiona Fenwick and took place on 30 September at Spy Valley Winery in Marlborough. The mentors and their mentees will now meet multiple times over the coming months.

summary:

content:
Last week, NSW Wine welcomed 17 wine show judges from across the country to the ICC Sydney to assess more than 750 wine entries entered into the 2026 ICC Sydney NSW Wine Awards.

The organisation said that, after “three enjoyable but intensive days”, it is pleased to share that 64 gold medals were awarded this year in 19 different classes.

“It was an incredibly fun and exciting couple of days at the ICC immersing ourselves into the brilliant world of NSW wines. As expected, the classic varieties of Shiraz and Chardonnay were exceptional. Semillon, both young and old, were world class and unique,” said chair of judges Adam Walls.

“Riesling was better than it has ever been and the sheer number of different varieties being made and entered captivated the judging team.”

The 2026 gold medal winning wines are now in the running for top varietal trophies and ‘Best Wine in NSW’ at this year’s awards, hosted at the ICC Sydney.

The 2026 NSW Wine Awards Ceremony, proudly supported by major event sponsor ICC Sydney, will be held on Friday 30 October 2026.

content:
Nicky and Sandy Oatley. Image credit Robert Palmer.

Treasury Wine Estates (TWE) has announced the sale of the Rosemount, Ingoldby and Secret Stone brands to A.G. Oatley Wines, owned by the Oatley family.

The company said the sale is the latest step in its transition to a more focused brand portfolio, following its recent sale of the Seppelt, Rouge Homme and Tollana brands to local owners.

“The sale will see Rosemount return to its founding family and forms part of TWE’s broader transformation agenda to condense its 76 brands to a priority portfolio of 30 global and regional brands,” it explained.

This includes investment to grow its ‘Power Brands’ (Penfolds, DAOU, Matua) and ‘Regional Heroes’ (Wynns, Pepperjack, Coldstream Hills, Squealing Pig, Frank Family Vineyards, Beaulieu Vineyard, and Stags’ Leap Winery) over the long term.

The three brands sold to the Oatley family. Images supplied

Angus Lilley, TWE managing director, Australia & New Zealand and Europe, said the sale was a positive outcome for the three brands.

“Since we announced our transformation agenda last year, we’ve sold five brands and a range of non-priority assets as we focus our investment and resources to grow in key markets,” Lilley said.

“The Oatleys bring deep experience in Australian wine and are well placed to take Rosemount, Ingoldby and Secret Stone into the future. We’ll work closely with them to ensure a smooth handover for customers.”

A.G. Oatley Wines owner, Sandy Oatley, said the winery is thrilled to bring Rosemount home to the family once more.

“I worked with my father building Rosemount into a globally recognised Australian brand for 20 years. To have the opportunity to now work on the brand with my daughter, Nicky, is an extraordinary full circle moment.”

The sale includes the three brands and associated inventory and is expected to complete on Friday 23 October 2026.

TWE will retain royalty-free rights to sell Rosemount in Europe for up to three years, with no immediate change to customer ordering arrangements in those markets.

A.G. Oatley announced days ago it had also purchased the Murray Street Vineyards.

“Our family has been involved in the industry for generations, and we remain incredibly passionate about Australian wine,” said Nicky Oatley.

“South Australia is such an important part of the industry’s future, and these investments in the Barossa Valley and McLaren Vale allow us to play a meaningful role.

“I’m excited to work with our director of winemaking, Larry Cherubino, to keep innovating, buoyed by our recent success of my own label ‘NOW’ (Nicole Oatley Wines), particularly our Swan Valley Chenin Blanc and Margaret River Cabernet Franc. And now, with Rosemount, it’s truly exciting to have the opportunity to work alongside my dad to reimagine a brand that holds such a special place in our hearts. We’re not quite ready to share what that looks like yet. For now, we’re just incredibly happy to have Rosemount back in the family and excited about what’s ahead.”

title: Wolf Blass AM named South Australian ‘Legend of the Vine’
summary:
Wine Communicators of Australia (WCA) announced Wolf Blass AM as the 2026 South Australian ‘Legend of the Vine’ on Friday (9 October) at the Royal Adelaide Wine Awards Lunch. The SA Legend of the Vine Award is presented by Wine Communicators of Australia to “recognise a South Australian who is of excellent character, who is held in high regard by their peers in the world of wine and who has made an outstanding contribution to the Australian wine industry”. “Wolf Blass is an outstanding Legend of the Vine, as he is a passionate wine communicator — someone who has taken the Australian wine message to the world, with clarity, conviction, and no shortage of personality,” said WCA. “There is one spot left on the walls of my Gallery & Museum, so I know exactly where this certificate is going,” Blass said whilst accepting the honour.

The post Wolf Blass AM named South Australian ‘Legend of the Vine’ appeared first on Winetitles.
content:
LTR: Bill Hardy OAM and Wolf Blass AM. Image supplied

Wine Communicators of Australia (WCA) announced Wolf Blass AM as the 2026 South Australian ‘Legend of the Vine’ on Friday (9 October) at the Royal Adelaide Wine Awards Lunch.

The SA Legend of the Vine Award is presented by Wine Communicators of Australia to “recognise a South Australian who is of excellent character, who is held in high regard by their peers in the world of wine and who has made an outstanding contribution to the Australian wine industry”. The recipient “must also demonstrably share WCA’s values on the importance of developing and inspiring excellence in how they communicate about wine”.

“Wolf Blass is an outstanding Legend of the Vine, as he is a passionate wine communicator — someone who has taken the Australian wine message to the world, with clarity, conviction, and no shortage of personality,” said WCA.

Blass started his wine journey in Germany, where he completed a Certificate in Viticulture and Winemaking in 1952, followed by a Diploma in Oenology in 1954 and a Kellermeister qualification in 1956. But Australia soon called — and, in 1961, he moved to the Barossa, “beginning a career that would reshape the Australian wine story forever”.

In 1967, he introduced a colour-coded tiered label system for his wines — Grey, Yellow, Red, Black, Platinum — making wine “more accessible, less intimidating and far easier for everyday drinkers to understand”. WCA explained that this simple but brilliant communication breakthrough changed how Australians talked about wine.

His wines have dominated national awards with over 10,000 wins, including an unprecedented three consecutive ‘Jimmy Watson Trophies’ from 1974 to 1976, and again in 1999. No other producer has managed to win the trophy four times.

He has previously been recognised as a ‘Baron of the Barossa’, a ‘Member of the Order of Australia’, a ‘Senior Australian of the Year’ finalist and received the ‘Australian Export Hero Award’.

Beyond the bottle, WCA said Blass’s philanthropic footprint is extraordinary, with major contributions to sporting, cultural and community organisations across South Australia. In 1994, on his 60th birthday, he founded the ‘Wolf Blass Foundation’ which now has a permanent home at the Wolf Blass Gallery & Museum in Hahndorf.

“There is one spot left on the walls of my Gallery & Museum, so I know exactly where this certificate is going,” Blass said whilst accepting the honour.

Wolf is the twelfth South Australian to receive the SA Legend of the Vine Award. He joins a prestigious list that includes Prue Henschke, Jane Ferrari, Peter Hayes, Brian Croser AO, Pam Dunsford, Tony Love, Brian Walsh, d’Arry Osborne, Dr Patrick Iland OAM and Bill Hardy OAM, who presented Wolf with the Award Certificate on Friday.

title: The Wright take on how Fiano’s breaking into the mainstream
summary:
With Fiano Day around the corner (Friday 16 October), Daily Wine News took a trip to McLaren Vale and sat down with Corrina Wright, winemaker and director at Oliver’s Taranga Vineyards, to learn more about the alternative white that’s causing quite the buzz. content:
Corrina Wright, winemaker and director at Oliver’s Taranga Vineyards. Image supplied

By Kyra Trussell

With Fiano Day around the corner (Friday 16 October), Daily Wine News took a trip to McLaren Vale and sat down with Corrina Wright, winemaker and director at Oliver’s Taranga Vineyards, to learn more about the alternative white that’s causing quite the buzz.

Last year, Oliver’s Taranga Vineyards worked with Mastermind Consulting to develop the inaugural Fiano Festa and Fiano Day with the intention of encouraging consumers to learn more about the category.

“We thought there were about 80 producers, but we’ve now found that there’s about 300 producers of Fiano across Australia,” Wright explained.

Surprisingly, Fiano is planted in diverse regions all over the country, from Geographe in WA to the Hunter Valley in NSW.

“You’d be hard pressed to find a restaurant locally in South Australia that doesn’t have Fiano on the list now, and that is spreading to the eastern seaboard and over in the west as well.”

Moreover, at the recently held 2026 Royal Adelaide Wine Awards Lunch, chair of judges Samantha Connew explained that Fiano entries in the competition had increased from seven previously to a whopping 43 this year. With even Dan Murphy’s stocking a Fiano section now, it seems this once obscure Mediterranean grape variety is becoming an Aussie crowd-pleaser.

Wright suggested that this could be because the variety is attractive on several different fronts for the industry.

“I think grapegrowers have enjoyed it because of the disease tolerance, heat tolerance and drought tolerance. It has been hard some years to get set right, so a lot of us have moved to cane pruning, as it is in Italy. For the winemaker, Fiano has high natural acidity and thick skins full of flavour with low disease pressure and all those sorts of things make it really attractive.

“I think stylistically with food matching, it works really, really well. Sommeliers really love it and restauranteurs love it because it sort of sits in with their food really beautifully. Plus, it’s slightly easier to say than Falanghina [for example], so people aren’t as scared to order it.”

Wright described Fiano as a textural wine, with a nutty and leafy taste.

“People often talk about things like basil pesto as a descriptor. So, if you think about the creaminess of pine nuts or cashew nuts, or that type of flavour on the palate, with a little bit of leafiness and a little bit of lift. But sometimes, I talk about cured lemon or preserved lemon, or even almost like a white cheesy type of character.

“It just reminds me of sitting in Italy eating pizza and pasta!” she exclaimed.

When asked if she thinks Fiano could become a mainstream variety soon, Wright expressed that she has faith in the possibility.

“Who knows? We’ll see, we might get graduated from the Alternative Varieties Wine Show one day, like Pinot Gris and Prosecco have. I think so, it’s definitely one that makes sense. It doesn’t make sense that we’ve only had Chardonnay, Riesling, Sauvignon Blanc and varieties like that as being sort of the only whites. None of those really suit McLaren Vale particularly well, while they’re amazing in the Adelaide Hills or cooler climates like Tassie or Victoria.

“There’s such a vast array of varieties from all over the place, but I do think Fiano’s one of the ones that really make sense for growers, winemakers and consumers,” she concluded.

The expansive vineyards at Oliver’s Taranga.

After finding out the sheer number of Fiano producers in Australia, Wright says the team behind Fiano Festa decided to make the event more of a collaborative effort.

“We thought, ‘right, instead of doing something that just promotes us, we want to be able to have all producers get on board to raise the profile of Fiano over the whole country’.”

This led to the creation of a trade page on Oliver’s Taranga website where wineries can download Fiano Festa assets, event information, key messages and Fiano facts.

“We’ve already heard from the Hunter [Valley] putting on a show up at Saddler’s Creek, and then we’ve also heard in Victoria Phaedrus Estate are putting on an event as well, so far. Last year, we ended up hearing from bottle shops that they’d sold our Fiano that day, so it was kind of fun!

“And then, in the lead up — we’ve been doing it all year to be honest — but we do #FianoFriday, even though hashtags don’t exist anymore,” she laughed.

Wright also spoke about ‘Fiano Fridays’, an opportunity for wineries to go deeper and talk in detail about the variety with their customers via social media.

As for the goals of the Fiano Festa celebrations, Wright hopes that it will encourage consumers to diversify their palates and try new styles from around the country.

“I think these events are important because, if we’re drinking less — which, is fine, let’s drink better, and let’s also explore the world of wine and not necessarily have to always drink the same thing. I think one of the fun things about wine is finding out something new, learning a new variety or learning a new flavour profile that you enjoy as well and chatting about it with your friends.

“Fiano is one of those varieties that work over lunch, they’re not the heaviest of styles if people are looking to move away from that. I just think it’s important to chat about it, and to have people supporting their local producers wherever they are.”

She revealed that Olivers Taranga Vineyards will also be releasing new wines ahead of Fiano Day.

“We’ll be releasing our new ‘The Hunt for Mrs Oliver’, which is a traditional method sparkling from 2023. We also have the ‘Anfore Fiano’, which is tiny little volume that’s been aged in terracotta, but there’s only 900 litres of that, so it’s super small, but super fun.”

title: South Australian winemakers claim 12 trophies at 2026 Royal Adelaide Wine Awards
summary:
South Australian wineries have claimed 12 of the 26 trophies on offer at the 2026 Royal Adelaide Wine Awards, with the Adelaide Hills having a strong result, taking out Best Pinot Noir and Best Sparkling Wine, while alternative varieties also featured among the highlights. Evans & Tate’s 2024 Redbrook Estate Chardonnay won the George Fairbrother Memorial Trophy for Most Outstanding White Wine in Show, while Berton Vineyards’ 2023 Metal Label The Black Shiraz Limited Release won the Max Schubert AM Trophy for Most Outstanding Red Wine in Show. The Governor’s Trophies for the best South Australian entries went to Naked Run Wines for its 2026 Place in Time Sevenhill Riesling and Serafino Wines for its 2024 Serafino Reserve Grenache. Both wines will be served at Government House at official engagements over the next 12 months. Sidewood Estate won Best Pinot Noir, while Simon Tolley Wines won Best Sparkling Wine. The alternative reds classes were another highlight, with The Pawn Wine Company winning Best Other Varietal Red for its 2025 Malbec.

The post South Australian winemakers claim 12 trophies at 2026 Royal Adelaide Wine Awards appeared first on Winetitles.
content:
South Australian wineries have claimed 12 of the 26 trophies on offer at the 2026 Royal Adelaide Wine Awards, with the Adelaide Hills having a strong result, taking out Best Pinot Noir and Best Sparkling Wine, while alternative varieties also featured among the highlights.

Evans & Tate’s 2024 Redbrook Estate Chardonnay won the George Fairbrother Memorial Trophy for Most Outstanding White Wine in Show, while Berton Vineyards’ 2023 Metal Label The Black Shiraz Limited Release won the Max Schubert AM Trophy for Most Outstanding Red Wine in Show.

The Governor’s Trophies for the best South Australian entries went to Naked Run Wines for its 2026 Place in Time Sevenhill Riesling and Serafino Wines for its 2024 Serafino Reserve Grenache. Both wines will be served at Government House at official engagements over the next 12 months.

Sidewood Estate won Best Pinot Noir, while Simon Tolley Wines won Best Sparkling Wine.

“These are categories that have traditionally been dominated by Tasmania, so it was great to see the Adelaide Hills feature so strongly this year,” chair of judges Samantha Connew said.

The alternative reds classes were another highlight, with The Pawn Wine Company winning Best Other Varietal Red for its 2025 Malbec.

“We’re seeing these categories become stronger and stronger, with winemakers having more experience with the varieties and greater vine age,” Connew said.

“There were beautiful examples of Tempranillos, Nero d’Avolas, Montepulcianos and Sangioveses.”

Fiano entries increased from seven last year to 43 this year.

“We know that winemakers have been exploring these different varieties for years now, so we’re starting to see the results of that coming through now,” Connew said.

The 2026 Riesling class was also a standout, with six golds awarded and 10 wines called back by the panel chairs to have another look.

“The 2026 Riesling class in particular was a real standout. It was thrilling to see such strong competition in this class. There were six golds awarded, but we had 10 lovely wines that the panel chairs called back to have another look at, which is just outstanding,” Connew said.

The awards also recognised the National Wine of Provenance, with Leo Buring winning the Gramp, Hardy, Hill-Smith Trophy for three vintages of its Leonay Riesling. Marie Clay was awarded the F Miller & Co Prize for Winemaker of the National Wine of Provenance.

The Royal Adelaide Wine Awards, formerly the Royal Adelaide Wine Show, was the first wine show to introduce provenance classes. This year, the classes were opened to sparkling wine for the first time.

“The provenance classes are such a joy for the judging panel. The Royal Adelaide Wine Awards was the first to introduce the provenance classes, and this year we opened them up to sparkling entries. We had two entries this year, but we’d love to see that grow next year,” Connew said.

Entries remained steady, despite pressure on participation at other capital city wine shows.

“Entries for the awards remained steady which is really pleasing because most capital city wine shows are feeling pressure in this area. I think it highlights how positively these awards are viewed by the industry,” Connew said.

Trophies went to wineries from four states, reflecting the diversity of entries and the depth of viticultural and winemaking talent across the country.

The Royal Adelaide Wine Awards is described by its organisers as Australia’s most prestigious wine competition, with hundreds of wineries entering each year. Wines are judged over four days by a panel of judges from across Australia, who determine the medal and trophy winners through what the organisers describe as a rigorous and independent judging process.

The post New series of industry podcast to focus on how connection supports the wellbeing of grapegrowers appeared first on Winetitles.
content:
The podcast will once again be hosted by Callum McPherson and Nick Ryan. Image supplied

The role connection plays in supporting the wellbeing of grapegrowers is at the heart of a new series of Healthy Minds, Healthy Vines launching Monday 12 October.

Developed by the Wine Grape Council of South Australia (WGCSA), series 4 “brings together ten conversations exploring the people, relationships and experiences that shape wellbeing in and around grape growing — from family and community to connection with the land, purpose, identity and navigating change”.

Returning hosts Callum McPherson and Nick Ryan are set to guide the conversations, “bringing together voices from across grapegrowing, wine and regional communities to explore the different ways people find connection, perspective and purpose”.

Series 4 will discuss the topics of:

  • ‘The Next Generation’ — education, new ideas, finding your voice and choosing your own path.
  • ‘People & Community’ — leadership, shared experience, stories and the connections that hold communities together.
  • ‘Land & Purpose’ — stewardship, farming, looking after the land and leaving something better behind.
  • ‘Change & What Comes Next’ — transition, risk, courage, perspective and finding your way through.

WGCSA CEO Lisa Bennier said that series 4 reflects the importance of connection at a time of significant change for South Australia’s grapegrowing community.

“Grapegrowers are navigating an incredibly challenging period, and there is no single experience or pathway through it. What these conversations show is the importance of staying connected — to our families, our communities, our land, our purpose and to each other.

“Series 4 brings together ten very different conversations, but each offers something we hope growers can relate to, learn from or simply recognise in their own experience,” Bennier said.

There will be 10 episodes in series 4 featuring 11 guests and each will be released weekly from Monday 12 October.

The podcast series will be accessible via all major streaming platforms including Apple Podcasts, Spotify, iHeart Radio and Audible.

content:
The Rosé was made in collaboration with Reece Hignell of Cakeboi. Image credit Megann Evans

Patisserie Wines is expanding its collection this Spring through its collaboration with renowned Australian pâtissier and founder of Cakeboi, Reece Hignell, launching a new wine inspired by one of his signature desserts: the Raspberry Lamington.

Created by Hignell and the Patisserie winemaking team, the new Patisserie Raspberry Lamington Rosé is said to have bright raspberry flavours layered with hints of coconut and vanilla, “while a delicate frizzante finish adds a gentle sparkle and texture reminiscent of a freshly baked sponge”.

Inspired by the “charm and elegance of a French pâtisserie”, Patisserie was launched in 2025 to “reimagine the wine experience through flavours inspired by beloved desserts and sweet treats”.

The winery said that this collaboration and new release continues that approach to winemaking.

“Patisserie, since launch, has been a fun flavour journey for all involved,” said Ross Marshall, managing director at Fourth Wave Wine.

“In seeking enjoyment and deliciousness above all, working with Reece was a wonderful chance to take the decadent drinks experience even further. Turning one of Australia’s most loved cakes — and a signature Cakeboi creation — into a sparkling wine will be a great addition to the Patisserie range.”

For Hignell, the overall collaboration provided an opportunity to bring his best-known creations into a new category.

Reece Hignell of Cakeboi. Image supplied

“The Raspberry Lamington has been one of my favourite signature cakes ever since I used to make it with my Nan, so the opportunity to bring it to life in a completely different way was incredibly exciting,” he said.

“I’ve worked closely with the Patisserie Wines team from the start, hands on in each stage of development ensuring the flavours people know and love like the bright raspberry jelly, hints of coconut and vanilla are captured in the wine. It’s fun, nostalgic and unlike anything I’ve tasted before.”

The winery said the Raspberry Lamington Rosé is true to its “playful approach to flavour” and is the latest addition to a growing collection of wines inspired by beloved desserts.

“From long lunches and celebrations to casual catch-ups with friends, the new release offers a playful conversation starter that reimagines a familiar favourite in a distinctly Patisserie way,” it said.

Patisserie Raspberry Lamington Rosé is now available at Dan Murphy stores nationally for an RRP of $26.99.
